newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Romania would see NATO snub as cynical -president.
newsitem.headline: Romania would see NATO snub as cynical -president.

text.p: Romania would consider exclusion from early NATO expansion as a "cynical" decision which ignores the alliance's strategic interests, President Emil Constantinescu said on Monday.

Addressing a NATO security forum in Prague, Constantinescu said Romania would be "not security consumers but security providers" by immediately strengthening the alliance's southern flank nearer the world's potential trouble spots.

U.S. President Bill Clinton's stance to back only Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic for invitations to enter NATO at a July 8-9 NATO summit in Madrid has irked European allies who support Romania and Slovenia's early inclusion in the planned expansion into the former East Bloc.

Constantinescu did not refer directly to Clinton's decision during a lengthy speech to ministers, senior officials and aspirants, concentrating instead on making a geopolitical and moral case for Romania's inclusion in NATO.

But when Dutch Defence Minister Joris Voorhoeve asked if Romanian citizens -- more than 70 percent of whom back joining NATO -- would be patient if excluded in the first wave of expansion, Constantaninescu pounced.
He said first-wave exclusion would be a "huge popular disappointment...which would be considered to be a cynical decision, incapable of analysing (NATO's) global interests."
Still, he said, the consolidation of Romania's democratic reforms would continue, even if the early invitation did not come.

The Romanian government has been intensifying diplomatic efforts, but senior U.S. officials say their position is firm because a larger expansion would be costly and politically difficult to sell at home.
Since NATO decisions are taken by consensus, and the U.S.-backed countries seem the only unanimous choices, the Madrid decisions are unlikely to go against Washington's wishes.

Still France and Italy -- the most ardent backers of Romania and Slovenia's inclusion respectively -- continue to pillory Clinton's decision, with the Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi calling it "a big mistake" at the Group of Seven Summit in Denver on Saturday.
Clinton said there should be "an open door" to other countries to join later and there should be "an extra outreach" to countries seen as likely next-round entrants.

Constantinescu said Romania had made tremendous strides in building a democratic society and free economy, had settled problems with all its neighbours, and would immediately strengthen NATO's geostrategic position.

He said strategic interests had shifted since the end of the Cold War, and better direct access to resources in the Baltic, Adriatic and Black seas were increasingly important and would lower dependence on Persian Gulf oil.
"This (North-South) axis can only be ensured through simultaneous accession to NATO of Poland, Slovenia, and Romania...linking the Baltic Sea to the Black Sea," Constantinescu said.

He said the simulataneous development of an "East-West NATO axis" encompassing Slovenia, Hungary, and Romania, "would play a stabilising role in the Balkan region" and strengthen the alliance's most vulnerable southern flank.

"In the medium and long term the threats to collective security which the alliance will have to face will come...from an arch of crisis comprising the Caucasus (mountains) central Asia, the Middle East, the (Persian) Gulf area, and north Africa," the Romanian president said.
